extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers preparing illustrated works (books, journals, and electronic publications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for preparing, crediting, placing, and formatting illustrations, charts, graphs, and tables for print and electronic scholarly/publisher production. Covers permissions, credit lines, list-of-illustrations, chart and table design, numbering, placement, and alignment conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissions for reproducing artwork and museum-owned works
rubrics_metrics.description: You must write to obtain written permission, as well as a print of the work, from the museum or person that owns it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain formal written permission and a print when reproducing copyrighted artworks or museum-owned works; the author is responsible for permissions though the publisher should be consulted about what needs permission and best practices (see related sections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Model releases for identifiable human subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: May not use a photograph or other portrayal of an identifiable human subject without the consent of that person or someone acting on his or her behalf (e.g., by means of a model release form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consent/model release is obtained for identifiable people; responsibility lies with the author (publisher should advise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult publisher about permissions for electronic as well as print publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it is the author’s responsibility, not the publisher’s, to obtain permissions, the publisher should be consulted about what needs permission and the best way to obtain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek publisher guidance especially for works appearing in both electronic and print formats; see specific sections for fuller discussion and for electronic-file requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of credit lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A credit line usually appears at the end of a caption, sometimes in parentheses or in different type (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Photographer’s name occasionally appears in small type parallel to bottom or side of photo; some permissions grantors stipulate placement with the illustration itself and may charge more if credit appears elsewhere—editorial discretion may be needed when grantor language conflicts with consistent usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stating single-source for many illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: If most or all of the illustrations in a work are from a single source, that fact may be stated in a note or, in a book, in the preface, acknowledgments, or on the copyright page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In heavily illustrated books, all credits may be listed together in back matter (or rarely front matter); check permissions because some grantors require credit adjacent to the illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing credits together when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In a heavily illustrated book, all credits are sometimes listed together in the back matter or, more rarely, in the front matter—sometimes as part of a list of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidated credit lists are acceptable but watch permission stipulations about placement; editorial discretion is allowed to honor grantor spirit vs letter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting author-created illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations created by the author do not need credit lines, though wording such as 'Photo by author' may be appropriate if other illustrations require credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multi-author works, specify the particular author where appropriate; professional courtesy suggests crediting creators even if not contractually required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit line content for copyrighted reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: An illustration reproduced from a published work under copyright always requires formal permission unless fair use or a blanket Creative Commons–type license applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit line should include author, title, publication details, and occasionally copyright date; include page or figure number; if the full work appears in bibliography, a shortened credit line may suffice; see publisher-specific instructions for material from commercial agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor permission-grantor requested credit language
rubrics_metrics.description: Some permissions grantors request specific language in the credit line; in a work with many illustrations, such language in one or two credit lines may conflict with consistent usage in the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise editorial discretion to follow the spirit rather than the letter when possible; if grantor is intractable, use the language requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting commissioned material
rubrics_metrics.description: Work commissioned by the author (maps, photographs, drawings, charts) is usually produced under a 'work made for hire' contract; even if no credit is required, professional courtesy dictates mentioning the creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit may be omitted only if signature is reproduced; examples: 'Map by Kevin Hand', 'Photograph by Ted Lacey'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting material obtained free of charge
rubrics_metrics.description: For material the author has obtained free and without restrictions on its use, the credit line may use the word 'courtesy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Photograph courtesy of Ford Motor Company.' Such material includes illustrations under certain Creative Commons licenses; consult license details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting public-domain material
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrations from works in the public domain may be reproduced without permission; for readers’ information, however, a credit line is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an informative credit (example given) even when no permission is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting agency material
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs of prints, drawings, paintings, and the like obtained from a commercial agency usually require a credit line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example credit forms: 'Woodcut from Historical Pictures Service, Chicago' or 'Photograph from Wide World Photos.' Follow agency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crediting adapted material and data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: An author creating an illustration adjusted from, or using data from, another source should credit that source for professional courtesy and readers’ information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the source of data or adaptation in caption or figure credit (e.g., 'Data from New York Zoological Park').

rubrics_metrics.name: When to include a list of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: For book-length printed works, include a list of illustrations when the illustrations are of intrinsic interest apart from the text; electronic works will often include a list as an aid to navigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In print, list of illustrations usually follows table of contents; a list may double as a list of credits if credits do not appear with illustrations themselves; shorten long captions to one or two lines in the list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shortening captions for lists of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the list of illustrations, long captions should be shortened to a single line (or two at the most).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise entry lines and include page numbers; examples show full caption vs list entry form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and appropriate use of charts (graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A chart (graph) is a device that presents data in a simple, comprehensible form—often along x and y axes—and should be used only if it summarizes the data more effectively than mere words can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charts are considered line art and should be numbered and labeled as figures; they should make sense on their own; consult Tufte for design; charts intended for black-and-white reproduction should not be created in color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency among charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two or more charts are used within a work, especially if they deal with comparable material, they should follow a consistent style in graphics and typography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of the same kind must be represented the same way across charts; different visual effects should only be used to distinguish elements, not just for variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axes and curves labeling and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the x (horizontal) and the y (vertical) axes should be labeled; curves are usually presented in graphically distinct forms—e.g., continuous line vs broken line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axes serve a function similar to column heads in a table; curve elements in bar or pie charts should be distinct; all such elements should be labeled or identified in a key or caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart color and fill usage for reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use black and white for curves or fills rather than shading or color unless your publisher allows shading or color in appropriately prepared electronic files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check publisher allowance for shading/color; otherwise prefer black-and-white alternatives for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chart titles and labels capitalization and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of a chart appears as part of the caption, immediately following the figure number, and is capitalized sentence-style; labels within a chart are normally lowercased (except proper nouns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If labels are phrases they may be capitalized sentence-style; labels may be explained in a caption as needed; compare with table title rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and symbols in chart labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations and symbols may be used in labels as long as they are easily recognizable or explained in a key or caption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose forms that are clear to intended readers (e.g., 'US$millions' vs 'US$M'); be consistent and provide explanations when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and planning for genealogical and pedigree charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Genealogical/pedigree charts require careful planning to illustrate relationships with minimal crossing of lines or extraneous data and to remain within a reproducible shape and size for print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fan-shaped pedigree charts and other non-axial relationship charts may need special arrangements to highlight multiple relationships while preserving readability and printability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table preparation and consultation with publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables are time-consuming to typeset and correct and should be designed and constructed with care; consult the publisher on appropriate number, size, and physical form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A table should be as simple as material allows and understandable on its own; text should highlight main points without duplicating table details; consult publisher for electronic file instructions and journal-specific rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of tables versus graphs or text
rubrics_metrics.description: A table is excellent for presenting many individual, similar facts so they are easy to scan and compare; in contexts where exact values are not essential, a graph or plain text may be more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer graphs/charts for trends and patterns, tables for exact values and comparisons; online tables can present more data than print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency among tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistency in style is indispensable both within one table and among several for easy comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use consistent titles, column heads, abbreviations, line spacing, indentation, fonts, rules, and distinguishing features across all tables in a work, except where specific tables require different devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table numbering separate from illustrations and citation by number
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should be numbered separately from any illustrations (table 1, table 2, etc.), and every table should be cited in the text by number rather than by location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In books with many tables or multi-author chapters, use double numeration by chapter (table 1.1, 1.2, etc.); follow order of appearance for numbering and first mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of tables relative to text and use of callouts
rubrics_metrics.description: A numbered table should appear as soon as possible after the first text reference to it; the author or editor must provide callouts in the manuscript indicating the preferred location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callouts (e.g., 'table 3 about here') are production instructions that do not appear in the published work; in print, most tables under a page appear at top or bottom; in electronic formats, tables may appear inline or as thumbnails linking to full tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table structure: parts and roles (stub, column heads, cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: A table normally consists of rows and columns; the top row defines column heads, the far left column is the stub, and their intersections are cells (data cells).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent variables usually presented in stub; ensure table makes sense on its own; see figure examples for anatomy of table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use horizontal and vertical rules sparingly in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce a clear, professional-looking table, rules should be used sparingly—many tables will require just three horizontal rules (top, below column heads, bottom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional horizontal rules may separate spanner heads or enclose cut-in heads; vertical rules seldom used except for doubled-up tables or very complex tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table titles: be succinct and avoid interpretive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Table titles should be as succinct as possible and should not suggest any interpretation of the data; titles should be in noun form and may be capitalized sentence-style or headline style consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show preferred phrasing; the title usually follows the table number on the same line; include units or statistical info parenthetically if important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parenthetical information in table titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Important explanatory or statistical information is often included in parentheses in a title and should be set in sentence style even if the main title uses headline style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More detailed information belongs in a note to the table rather than the title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column heads: brevity, sentence-style capitalization, and units
rubrics_metrics.description: Column heads should be as brief as possible and are best capitalized sentence-style; they may include unit indication in parentheses following the head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use abbreviations where space is at a premium if clear; the first column (stub) does not always require a head; if numbering columns for reference, use Arabic numerals in parentheses centered below the column head.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spanner heads (decked heads)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a table demands column heads of two or more levels, spanner heads (decked heads) are used with a spanner rule between spanner and column heads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spanner heads should seldom exceed two levels for ease of reading; use spanner rules to show which columns the spanner applies to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cut-in heads as subheads in tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut-in heads, spanning all columns but the first, may be used as subheads within a table and usually appear between horizontal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exceptionally long table with cut-in heads may be a candidate for division into two or more tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stub column head and entries guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The stub lists categories for which corresponding column information is given; if entries are self-explanatory a stub head may be omitted; stub entries are capitalized sentence-style and carry no end punctuation unless they are questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stub entries should be syntactically consistent; if all entries are of like kind a head is helpful (e.g., 'Characteristic' or 'Year'); some tables may not include a stub.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting stub subentries and hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Items in the stub may form sequential or classified lists with subheads; subentries should have first words capitalized and be indented or use typographic distinction (italics/roman) to show levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use indentation or italics to distinguish levels; no need for colons after main entries unless journal style requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runover lines in stub entries indentation
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no subentries, runover lines in stub entries should be indented (typically by one em); if there are indented subentries, runover lines must be more deeply indented than the lowest level of subentry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is extra space between rows, runovers may be set flush left; ensure consistent indentation for readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations in stub columns and definition requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols or abbreviations are acceptable in the stub where space is at a premium; nonstandard abbreviations must be defined in a table footnote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ditto marks for repeated information; use footnotes to define n.d., n/a, or other nonstandard abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting totals and subtotals in stubs
rubrics_metrics.description: When the word Total appears at the foot of the stub, it is often indented more deeply than the entries above or distinguished typographically (e.g., italics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtotals should be treated similarly; extra space or short rules sometimes appear above totals; be consistent and follow journal style where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table body and cell conventions (cell content and empty cells)
rubrics_metrics.description: The table body includes all rows, columns, and heads; cells may contain data or be empty. If a column head does not apply to a stub entry, leave cell blank or fill with an em dash or three ellipsis dots to indicate no data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate 'not applicable' (blank) from 'no data available' (em dash or ellipsis) or use defined abbreviations (n/a, n.d.) with notes; zero means literal zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix tables: handling repeated intersections
rubrics_metrics.description: In a matrix where stub entries equal column heads, cells that would repeat data may be left blank or marked with an em dash or ellipsis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether relational order matters; leave self-intersections blank or mark them consistently; provide explanatory note if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presenting multiple values in a single cell
rubrics_metrics.description: A single cell may contain two values with one in parentheses to allow fewer columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify such presentations in the column heading or a note so readers understand which values correspond to which measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of rows and cell entries relative to stubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Each cell in a row aligns with the stub entry to which it belongs; if stub entry occupies more than one line, cell entry normally aligns on the last line of the stub entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both stub and cells have multiple lines, align first lines throughout the table body; ensure visual consistency and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of column heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Column heads that share a row align on the baseline; if any head occupies more than one line, all heads in that row align on the last (lowest) line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each column head except the stub is normally centered on the longest cell entry; adjust alignment if centering gives unbalanced appearance; stub head and entries are always left aligned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of numbers within columns (decimal and digit alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers without decimal points are usually aligned on the last digit (ranged right); numbers with decimal points are typically aligned on the decimal point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For quantities <1.0, leading zeros need not be added in tables unless style prescribes; center the column of numerals within the column on the widest numeral; ellipses and em dashes are centered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment for columns consisting of words or phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearance governs left-right alignment for word columns; short entries may be centered, longer entries usually begin flush left; runover lines may be indented or aligned flush left with the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alignment for readability and consistency across the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and rules for totals, averages, and means
rubrics_metrics.description: Extra vertical space or short rules sometimes appear above totals but no rules should appear above averages or means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistency and follow journal/series style; the word 'Total' in the stub is often indented or typographically distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to include totals and handling rounding discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Totals and subtotals may be included if useful; when percentages in a column are based on different n’s, a final percentage based on total N may be informative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rounding can cause totals to sum to slightly more or less than 100; if given, show actual value (e.g., 99% or 101%) and explain discrepancy in a footnote.
